issue.issue_text: Whether the Land Customs Act, 1924 would apply to the Santhal Parganas on the ground that it is an existing law under Article 372 of the Constitution.

facts: The Santhal Parganas was an 'excluded or partially excluded area' under the Government of India Act, 1935.
Prior to the Constitution, laws like the Land Customs Act, 1924, did not automatically apply to these areas; they required a specific notification by the Governor to be put into force.
The Land Customs Act, 1924, had not been specifically made applicable to the Santhal Parganas before the Constitution came into effect.
law: Article 372(1) of the Constitution states that all 'laws in force' in the territory of India before the Constitution shall continue in force.
Explanation I to Article 372 clarifies that 'law in force' includes a law that existed but was not yet in operation in a particular area.
The Fifth Schedule of the Constitution deals with the administration of excluded and partially excluded areas.
application: The respondent argued that the Land Customs Act, 1924, was an 'existing law' for the territory of India and, under Article 372, it automatically became applicable to the Santhal Parganas after the Constitution commenced, as the old restrictions (like needing a Governor's notification) were no longer operative.
The Supreme Court rejected this interpretation. It reasoned that Article 372 and its Explanation I were designed to preserve the legal status quo as it existed before the Constitution.
The Court distinguished between laws that were in force in excluded areas and laws that were in force in the rest of India.

It held that Article 372 saves laws that were existing in territories *other than* excluded areas for those territories, and it saves laws that were existing in excluded areas *for those specific areas*.

Crucially, the Court determined that a law that was an 'existing law' for the rest of India did not automatically become an 'existing law' under Article 372 for an excluded area where it had never been applied.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the Land Customs Act, 1924, was not in force in the Santhal Parganas before the Constitution, it did not qualify as an 'existing law' for that specific area under Article 372. Therefore, the Act did not apply to the Santhal Parganas on this ground.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Bihar Regulation I of 1951 is in excess of the Governor's powers.

facts: The Governor of Bihar enacted Bihar Regulation I of 1951, which made the Imports and Exports Control Act, 1947, applicable to the Santhal Parganas.
The Santhal Parganas are a 'Scheduled Area' as defined under Article 244 and the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution.
The appellants challenged this regulation, contending that it was beyond the scope of the Governor's powers.
law: Under Article 244 and Paragraph 5 of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution, the Governor has special powers regarding laws applicable to Scheduled Areas.
Paragraph 5(2) of the Fifth Schedule empowers the Governor to make regulations for the peace and good government of a Scheduled Area.
Paragraph 5(3) of the Fifth Schedule grants the Governor the power to repeal or amend any Act of Parliament or State Legislature that applies to the area.
application: The Court rejected the argument that the Governor's power to 'make regulations' does not include the power to 'apply' a law made by another legislature.
It held that the power to make regulations is a full legislative power that 'embraces the utmost power to make laws and to apply laws.'
The Court reasoned that applying a law to an area is a recognized form of legislation and is equivalent to making a law for that area.
Furthermore, the Court found that the power to apply laws is inherent in the Governor's authority to repeal or amend existing Acts, as granted by Paragraph 5(3).

The Court also dismissed the contention that the regulation was a piece of delegated or conditional legislation, stating instead that the Governor was exercising a primary legislative authority in its 'plenitude of power' for the Scheduled Area.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Bihar Regulation I of 1951 was a valid exercise of the Governor's legislative authority under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution. The Governor's power to make regulations for a Scheduled Area includes the power to apply existing laws, and therefore, the regulation was not in excess of the Governor's powers.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Land Customs Act, 1924 would apply to the Santhal Parganas on the ground that it is an existing law under Article 372 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The Land Customs Act, 1924 did not apply to the place of occurrence (Santhal Parganas).
respondent_arguments: The Land Customs Act, 1924 became applicable to excluded areas like Santhal Parganas after the Constitution because it was an 'existing law' under Article 372.

The restriction under section 92 of the Government of India Act, 1935, which required a specific declaration by the Governor to apply legislation to these areas, was no longer operative after the Constitution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Bihar Regulation I of 1951 is in excess of the Governor's powers.
appellant_arguments: The Governor's power to apply laws under the Fifth Schedule is synonymous with conditional legislation, implying the Bihar Regulation I of 1951 was an improper exercise of this power.
respondent_arguments: The Bihar Regulation I of 1951 is not a piece of delegated or conditional legislation.
The Governor had full power under the Fifth Schedule to make regulations which are laws, just as Parliament can enact legislation for a particular area.

cases.principle: The effect of bringing clauses of a former Act into a subsequent Act is to write those sections into the new Act as if they had been enacted in it for the first time.

cases.case_name: The Secretary of State for India in Council v. Hindustan Co-operative Insurance Society Ltd.
cases.principle: When an Act incorporates provisions from an existing Act by reference, it does not bind itself to any future amendments made to the incorporated Act, as the provisions are adopted as they existed at the time of incorporation.

A notification issued under one act (e.g., Foreign Exchange Regulation Act) can be deemed to be a notification under Section 19 of the Sea Customs Act, and a contravention of such a notification attracts each and every provision of the Sea Customs Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Governor's power to make regulations for scheduled areas under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution is a full and plenary legislative power, not a form of delegated or conditional legislation. When a statute incorporates the provisions of an earlier Act, the legal effect is to write those provisions into the new Act as if they were enacted in it for the first time. Furthermore, under Article 372, laws that were existing in the general territory of India but not in excluded or partially excluded areas before the Constitution do not automatically become law in those areas.
